utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Simic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. It's your case. May the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Grujicic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Good morning. I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, when we spoke previously, I already told you how this examination should proceed: To speak slowly and to wait before answering my question. There will be a pause anyway, because this is a videolink, but we don't want your answers and my questions to overlap. I will also tell you that the Trial Chamber is aware of your health condition. I was informed yesterday by my colleague Mr. Krgovic that you feel well now. So now, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, and in my own name, I wish to say that if at any point in time you don't feel well, please feel free to say so, and we are going to take a break then, primarily in the interests of your health.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to work my way through your c.v., and then I'm going to put leading questions to you, so that we would go through this a bit more quickly. And in part, I'm going to ask you for very precise answers to some questions. Could you please slowly state your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: My name is Milutin Grujicic. I was born in 1935, in Jasenovac, municipality of Novska, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Just pause for a second. Could you please give us your marital status. Are you married? Do you have a family?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married. My wife's name is Zorica. My father and mother have died.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, could you please tell us what your ethnic background is.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to present what I know about your c.v. now, and you're going to tell me whether that is accurate. You have completed teacher's college in Krizevici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You completed the academy of Pedagosku in Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both towns are in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked as a teacher throughout your career, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I wish to add that I also obtained a university degree in political science, in Zagreb, and I studied at the department for all National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you get this university degree? Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were a teacher in Virovitica, in Novi Gradiska, in Okucani; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spent a certain period of time as a teacher at the Stara Gradiska house of corrections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I was there as a teacher and a penologist. I had to deal with convicts who were multiple offenders. I was director of the schooling centre for convicted persons. There was an elementary school and there was a secondary school.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end because of what the attorney said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In May 1987, you retired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us note one more thing in relation to your c.v., you were an active sportsman. You were a referee in handball, and for many years you were president of the cultural and arts society in Okucani; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. A handball referee, coach, and player. That's what I did in Virovitica and Novi Gradiska. As for the culture and arts society, I was in charge of that in Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it is noteworthy for this Trial Chamber to refer to another thing from your c.v. Mr. Grujicic, you have been a writer as well, a non-fiction writer. Could you tell us what you've been writing about?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. First, as a teacher, I wrote professional papers and various periodicals. I also worked as a journalist for the local radio station of Novi Gradiska and the local paper. After this civil war, that is to say, after the exchanges, I wrote two books. One is called "Listen, country. I'm confessing to you." And the second one is called "The graves of war hurt." I've been trying to write other things too in order to establish the truth, to see where 24.000 missing persons are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you do your military service? When? Which year? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody remembers that. In 1958, towards the end of March, I went to the reserve officers' school in Zadar. I completed this reserve officers' school, and then I was sent to Backa Topola. I returned to [as interpreted] the army and I continued to work in Okucani. I'm a reserve officer, a Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. There is an intervention to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The witness said I returned from the army, not to the army. It's on page 4, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, one more question related to your c.v. Were you ever a member of a political party, and are you one now?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about before? Were you ever a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. However, when my party betrayed me, I stopped being a member, and I am no longer a member of any political party, except for one thing: I always think about humanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear. After you stopped being a member in the League of Communists, you never joined any other party?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Never. Never. I never joined up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, we asked you to come here as a witness to talk about the process of exchanges that you participated in and about your knowledge related to what my client, Mr. Miroslav Tadic, did in the field of exchanges. So I would like to ask you now first to tell us: How come you actually got involved in the process of exchanges, and when this took place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: This took place in 1991, when the unfortunate civil war broke out in Croatia, in my area, between the Serbs and the Croats. It happened that three days after the war broke out, there were already persons who were dead or taken prisoner. I must say that on both sides there were my pupils. I was afraid for both, because they were taken prisoner, and I remembered that the only exchange was carried out in 1942, in Okucani, between the partisans and the Ustashas. That was the first exchange in world ever since there has been warfare, that during the actual course of a war there is an exchange between the warring parties involved. I immediately addressed the command of the Territorial Defence in Okucani that I belonged to as well, and I suggested to them that we telephone our friends and colleagues who had been our friends and colleagues only until yesterday but who now belonged to the other side, those who were from Gradiska, and that we should offer them an exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What number of persons was involved? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. At that moment, three of our people were taken prisoner, and one of their people. I can also give you the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to go into detail.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: This was the 17th of August, 1991. Mr. Miroslav Cupic, who I proposed this to, was president of the Crisis Staff in Novi Gradiska. He said that as soon as he agreed with the army - and he believed that it would be all right - he would let me know whether our proposal was accepted, and indeed our proposal was accepted. We carried out the first exchange in this civil war, the first official exchange, on the 28th of August, 1991, and since then, exchanges started. As an ongoing form of exchange between the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Chamber - you've already mentioned it, but were you then part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I was involved in the Territorial Defence. I was 57 years old at the time, and I had health problems even then, though of a different kind, and of course I agreed to do whatever I could and what I felt in my heart that I should do in a case such as that. So I was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you join the military commission, and what was the first military commission you joined? Could you tell the Chamber briefly when this was and what this commission was competent for.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Let's understand each other. A member of the Territorial Defence is, by definition, a member of the JNA. It's true that I was wearing civilian clothes, but on the 1st of January, 1992, the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Okucani was deployed in the units of the 5th Banja Luka Corps. General Talic suggested to me that I become part of the commission of the Banja Luka Corps because he had heard of my previous work in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a minute, please. Tell us: The 5th Banja Luka Corps, what army was that part of at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army, and on the 19th of May, I think, 1992, the Yugoslav People's Army was withdrawn and the army of Republika Srpska was established. Therefore, I began my work in the Yugoslav People's Army, and I continued it in the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall talk about your work in that commission, but now please tell me -- I would like to put a few questions to you about the period before your work in the commission of the 1st Krajina Corps. You have already told us that from August 1991, you worked on the first exchange, in the period from August 1991 and throughout the first few months of 1992, did you work on exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: All the time I worked on exchanges, which means from the 17th of August, 1991 until 1995. However, up to 1992, I worked in a commission with active-duty officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go into that later.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: -- but exchanges took place all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In these exchanges in the first period, were representatives of international organisations present, and do you remember who escorted the first exchanges? I'm referring to international institutions. Who monitored them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: During the first exchanges, the European Mission was there, and they were there as monitors. They did not get involved in our work or in the negotiations. They simply monitored what was going on. They had their own interpreters, who interpreted to them our conversations. They wore white uniforms, and we were glad of this, because, for the most part, we were on no man's land between two front lines, and the European Mission in white uniforms could be seen from afar. So we found them very useful. That's as far as the beginning is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Did the International Red Cross get involved, and if so, when? And does the name Heidi Huber mean anything to you? Can you tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The exchanges took place, but sometimes they could not take place on the territory of Western Slavonia. In those cases, we went to Bosnia and Herzegovina and exchanged people across the river Sava. This created difficulties for us. I heard that in Sarajevo there was a lady who was a representative of the International Red Cross, and her name was Heidi Huber. I obtained her telephone number and address. I sent her an official letter saying that I wanted us to meet in Bosanska Gradiska so that I could get to know her and ask her for help, because I was aware of the amount of help that the International Red Cross could provide. She came to the meeting in Bosanska Gradiska and we reached an agreement, but as there was still no war in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- I mean to say we kept in touch with her. And as soon as war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I asked her, if at all possible, that an office of the International Red Cross be opened in Banja Luka. This was closer to us, and we needed it to facilitate our cooperation. And I assume that she informed her superiors of this, and very soon an office was opened in Banja Luka. And then our work went on more smoothly and more expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify for the Chamber, and we will go into this later on: You were a member and president of the commission of the 1st Krajina Corps. Could you please tell the Chamber where the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps was.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The headquarters was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Later on, our office was also in Banja Luka, in the corps command. The International Red Cross was about 300 metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we are discussing the International Red Cross, please tell us whether you addressed them and whether they organised any seminars in connection with your work.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The International Red Cross organised a seminar in Banja Luka, pursuant to an agreement between the gentleman from the International Red Cross and me, and I was already the president of the commission for the exchange of war prisoners and civilians of the 1st Krajina Corps, and we were co-organisers, so to speak. The meeting was held in the -- on the premises of the corps, and the lecturers were representatives of the International Red Cross. They brought files with material for each participant. We had tests to fill in. And in agreement with the representatives of the ICRC, I invited all the members of the military commission, all the members of those municipalities which had civilian commissions and which did not have representatives of municipal committees of the Red Cross. This seminar was very successful, and it was also attended by Mr. Miroslav Tadic, among other people, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move on to your membership and your appointment as president of the commission of the 1st Krajina Corps. You have already said that after the Yugoslav People's Army left on the 19th of May, the army of Republika Srpska was established and the 1st Krajina Corps. Do you remember when you were appointed president of the commission? And I'm especially interested in what led up to this reorganisation of the commission, according to your knowledge, of course.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: First, I was a member of a commission comprising active-duty officers, and I was the only one there whose only duty this was. And I was the one who initiated constant requests for searches for the imprisoned and those who had been killed. But the active-duty officers were on positions with their duties -- with their units, and this was a burden to them. At the time, I was not yet the president of the commission, and I felt helpless. I wanted to do much more than I was able to do, because it became evident in Okucani that a lot could be done if one was willing. At a certain point, I suggested to General Talic that it might be a good idea if the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war comprised civilians from the entire territory where the front line was, to facilitate the work of the commission, to help in collecting information, and to make it easier for the commission to do its job. He ordered me to put down my proposal in writing, and I did so, and I listed the kinds of professions that were to be represented in the commission for exchanges. At my proposal, the civilian commission was then established, and sometime in May I was appointed president of the commission for exchanges. But at that time, there was still two officers and one lawyer in the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask the registrar to show the witness document PDB 17/3. I have prepared copies for the Chamber of all the documents I wish to tender through this witness. There are some 14 or 15 documents in total. I disclosed these documents to the OTP a long time ago, and yesterday I talked to Mr. David Re again about these documents. And if there is no objection, after the OTP could perhaps tell us their position when the first document is introduced so that we could proceed relatively quickly. The first of the documents that I wish to discuss is the document that I hope you have been shown now, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just confirm to me that we are looking at the same document, please. This is a document dated the 29th of May, 1992, and it's an order on the establishment of the commission for exchanges, signed by General Major Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Is this the document appointing you president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document where I was appointed president of the commission, along with two officers, Veljko Grbic, a major; and Major Novak Djokovic; and Zoran Opacic, a conscript, was a lawyer, and he worked in the legal service of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Just a moment, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our clients are saying they cannot see the document. Let me see if I have a copy for them. [In English] Ms. Usher, a copy at the ELMO, just for the benefit of our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, you see this now?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's not very sharp. If you could raise it up a little bit. Yes. Yes. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if you were to look directly at the document, if that's technically possible.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I see the document on the ELMO, and I also see it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excellent. In the preamble, what it says here, it says that in view of weaknesses noticed in the work of the commission. Is this what you have just been telling us about the problems in the previous work of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is it. Because this commission, as I said, couldn't carry out its humane task, so I drew up this proposal. But this order is in fact an interim solution --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go into this later.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: -- until what I proposed could be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see in the first paragraph, after the appointment of the members of the commission, it says that only the president of the commission will do this job full time. Does this mean that you, Mr. Grujicic, did only exchange work after your appointment as president of this commission?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I only did work on exchanges. I had a lot of help from Zoran Opacic, and less help from the active-duty officers, because they were at their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to us now what it says in the third paragraph: "The commission will keep records and realise full cooperation with the ICRC and all those who can help in searches." What was the task of the commission in relation to these civilian institutions mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: The commission will cooperate. This means -- it was wartime, so I was not able to go over to the other side and say to them: Are our prisoners of war here? But on the basis of conversations with people and the municipal committees of the Red Cross, and all possible structures, we cooperated so that we could learn about the imprisoned, the missing, and the dead, as soon as possible and as easily as possible. In the field, this was well understood, so that in many municipalities which were directly exposed to the front line, civilian commissions were set up. Where there were no civilian commissions, there was the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Besides this, we learned about the imprisoned, the missing, and the dead through prisoners who had been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: So no army can be without its people if it wants to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Never mind. We'll talk about that later. Just tell me one thing, in order to understand this document fully. The last sentence, assistant commander for MV and PP. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for moral training is Milutin Vukelic from Banja Luka. Nowadays he's a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what does "PP" mean?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, at this moment I can't remember myself. I'll have to give it some thought, and perhaps I'll remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Is that perhaps legal issues, "pravna pitanja"?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No. It is legal affairs, "pravni poslovi."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was actually guessing too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Your Honours, if there is no objection from the Prosecution, I would like to have this document tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D169/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Grujicic: In addition to your commission, were there other military commissions for exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: In the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were military commissions in all corps. There were six corps and six military commissions. At the level of Republika Srpska, there was a central commission too, which brought together civilian and military commissions. And I've already said this, actually: There were civilian commissions. And in the Republic of Croatia, because we still worked with them too, there was a single commission for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: In the regions, such as the Banja Luka region and the Krajina region, there was also a regional civilian commission, also in the other regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would particularly be interested in the interdependence between all the institutions that you've referred to. First of all, I'm interested in the relationship between military commissions at the same level. So what kind of relationship was there, and was there a relationship between the 1st Krajina Corps and the East Bosnian Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, it is only natural that we had good relations with the military corps that bordered on us, that is to say, the East Bosnian Corps, with its headquarters in Bijeljina. Later on, when the 2nd Krajina Corps was established, I was sent there to help them with this. Their seat was in Drvar, and of course we had cooperation with them too. As for the Drina Corps from Zvornik, we had this too, whereas the other corps that are geographically remote, it was only that we could communicate by fax, seeking information about missing persons. Cooperation was, quite simply, necessary, in view of the fact that we were dealing with the same regions. For example, the East Bosnian, the Zvornik, and us, we all had to deal with the Tuzla region. It was not important who would carry out the exchange, Banja Luka, Bijeljina, or Zvornik, who would exchange which prisoners. We would simply reach agreement on this, based on the request put forth by the other side. So we worked in concordance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to what you've said just now, I would like you to have a look at a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown document PDB 98/3. This is a letter dated the 3rd of April, 1993. It is addressed to Lieutenant Matija Bodirogic in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have that document before you, Mr. Grujicic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. My first question: Is this your signature? Are you the signatory of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: It is my signature. I wrote the letter. No one could sign a letter on behalf of the commission for exchanges of the 1st Krajina Corps except for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this document. Is this what you've been talking about? Do the contents of this letter show this cooperation? First tell me: Who was Matija Bodirogic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: A lieutenant, reserve lieutenant. Matija Bodirogic was president of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war of the East Bosnian Corps from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this -- I mean, the document itself is self-explanatory, but is this what you refer to? Does this reflect your cooperation and the relations between the military commissions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on the basis of agreements reached. We would always reach agreements as to who should do what, either vis-a-vis the Main Staff, because there can be no exchanges without the Main Staff, without the legal services, that is to say, without the judiciary or, rather, the core legal organs. And it is only when we would receive these documents that we could approach a prison, so we had to reach agreement on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, Maksim Simeunovic is referred to. Tell me: You could tell us what he did and whether you had cooperation with this man often. We here are familiar with this person.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mato [as interpreted] Simeunovic was a member of the commission of the East Bosnian Corps. He was in Brcko. I admire the calm way in which he worked. I admire his sense of responsibility and his great care for missing persons. So Makso Simeunovic was a link between our two corps. As the Samac commission was -- well, we'll deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I have to correct the transcript. The name is wrong. Page 18, line 5, it says, "Mato," but Makso is the word you used. That was his nickname; right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Makso. His real name was Maksim, and we called him Makso.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who is the person mentioned in the last paragraph, Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I see. In every commission there was a member and a security officer -- that is to say, the security officer of that particular corps. In this case, Mr. Mitrovic was the security officer of the East Bosnian Corps. In order to carry out these duties as easily as possible, by way of reaching agreement at commission level, he had the task of communicating with the security service in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a number for this document, if the Prosecution does not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go ahead?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D170/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next question: You've already referred to a central commission that existed, a state commission. Where was the seat of this commission? Do you know? And there's another thing I'm interested in -- well, let's do this one by one. Where was the seat of the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The seat of the commission was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know who were the members of this commission? Were these military personnel or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The president of the commission was reserve Captain Dragan Bulajic, and in the commission there was also a representative of the Main Staff, an officer from the Main Staff. He was liaison. He was coordinator between the commission and the Main Staff, and there were certain civilians who were members of this commission or, rather, military conscripts, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in this commission there were persons who cooperated with the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska or who worked there? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in every commission there were lawyers too, so I am a teacher by vocation, and certainly I'm not very well versed in this. Perhaps I know a bit, because I worked in this kind of service. But a lawyer is a lawyer. This is a professional thing. So basically, he was supposed to cooperate with the judiciary organs, with the investigators, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell the Trial Chamber: What was the relationship between this central commission and your military commissions? How did this function?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, there was a war. This did not always function very well. But specifically, our commission - and I know the East Bosnian commission very well too - we enjoyed the support of our command, and we worked on the basis of approval. If we did not have communications right at that moment, and if the persons we were exchanging were not really troublesome, if I can put it that way, except if somebody was under investigation or was sentenced, then our command couldn't do a thing. That was only natural. Then our republican commission said that if somebody had been sentenced already, the president of the republic could amnesty such a person for this exchange that was involved, or the president could pardon a person who was under investigation so that the exchange could take place. But this was also done by the commission at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What was your experience, Mr. Grujicic, in that work on exchanges? We heard that for a long number of -- for a long time you worked on this. What was your experience with politicians if they worked on exchanges and in this line of work?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I said that I was the first person to start exchanges in this war, and I have given deep thought to the matter. I thought that only persons who feel the misfortune of those who need help - namely, prisoners - only such persons could be involved in this line of work, only humanists could do this. It would often happen that in various capacities, not as permanent members, there were politicians who would rush into this kind of thing. Then we'd really have problems, because politicians from either side would sort of go -- would function on a tit-for-tat basis. If somebody would say something, the other one would hasten to return. So then no exchange could be carried out. I proposed to all humanists that we should work out a code, a humane code, that no one could be engaged in exchanges except for us who really wanted the persons who were imprisoned to be exchanged, and those who really wanted to look for missing persons. So we eliminated politicians. I specifically had the possibility of issuing an order to the soldiers on the front line that such-and-such a person could not go through. It was the same on the other side. So everyone who would be entering no man's land would have to be recorded in the list that I would send to certain organs with my signature. So politicians were never welcome. We never found them welcome in these -- in this particular line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, tell me -- or, rather, tell the Trial Chamber: What did your commission do? Who did you exchange? Who did you reach decisions about?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The subject of work of our commission was the exchange of prisoners of war, looking for missing persons and looking for persons who were killed. However, sometimes it would happen that we would have to deal with civilian persons as well. Although we had a principle there that civilian persons -- or, rather, that corridors should be established and that civilians should have unhindered passage both ways, in order to have families reunited. Or, for example, students, pupils who happened to be in towns, sick persons, all these people simply happened to be in a war zone. And I already said that with civilian persons, we had various situations. For example, if people from the other side would try to move through a minefield to move on to our side, then they would usually call us to handle that particular line of work, or rather, to help these people. These are civilian persons. For example, I remember well at Bugojno, a little girl got killed. One passed to the other side and some other civilians too. They informed us from Donji Vakuf. We first of all fed these people, and then we took them to the Croatian side, because they wished to go to Croatia. We handed them over at Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your commission have any rules of procedure, and what was the legal basis for the work of your commission?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: First, the East Bosnia Corps drew up a proposal, or rather, a draft rules of procedure, for the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war. Our colleagues submitted this to us and we adapted it to suit the conditions we were working in, in the Banja Luka region. We then compiled rules of procedure, but I don't have them in my possession. I left them behind in the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to inform the Chamber that I do have these rules of procedure from 1994. They fall outside the time limits of the indictment, so I will not enter them here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We drew up these rules, and they were signed by General Talic, Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, although you've already mentioned this, but tell us in detail: The principle of exchange was negotiating searching for people on both sides, asking for people to be exchanged. Tell us: On receipt of a request from the other side, what was your procedure? What approval did you have to seek? You mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: When we received a request from the opposite side, that is, a list of names of people they were looking for, first we would check whether these persons were in prison. If they were not in prison, we would ring up the East Bosnia Corps to see whether they were being held in Batkovic If they weren't there either, we would then mark the names those who were not in the prisons of the two corps. Those who were in one of these two prisons would be listed by us, and we would send this list to the public prosecutor. The investigations department and the Court, to see what the status of each particular prisoner was. On receipt of the reply, we would submit this to the security service. The security service of our corps would submit this to the security service of the Main Staff. If someone had been convicted, after approval from the Main Staff, we would ask for a document from the president of the Republic, or other organs, so that this prisoner could be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like two documents to be shown to you. One is PDB 78/3. This is a telegram from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, dated the 4th of January -- the 14th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, will you tell us, please, what institution is writing this, whom it is addressing, and who is the person who signed this telegram.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: All the activities I have just mentioned had been carried out by us. Lists had been submitted to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, asking for approval for this exchange, and pursuant to our document, they sent us a reply, and this was signed by the chief, General Major -- Major General Manojlo Milovanovic, because General Tolimir wasn't there at the moment and it was he who was in charge of security usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be given a number first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked as D171/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is PDB 80/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, dated the 21st of January, 1993, and is signed by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. Tell us: Who is writing? Whose signed is this [as interpreted], what you have just mentioned, the person who, for the most part, issued these approvals?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is another exchange. But again, on the basis of clarification of all situations, we sent a request for exchange, and Colonel Zdravko Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. We had some technical problems. Can you tell us who Mr. Zdravko Tolimir is?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zdravko Tolimir was a colonel, and he was the chief of the service or administration for intelligence and security work in the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. And pursuant to our request, he sent us approval for the exchange we had proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this same principle apply in every exchange you carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively. There was no exchange without approval. The army said that everything had to be done according to the rules of service. Every exchange, therefore, had to be approved. When an exchange was carried out, we had signed lists, and with these, we crossed the lines into no man's land. No one was able to go there who was not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D172/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more document connected to this topic. Could the witness be shown document P127/3 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is also a telegram from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, dated the 9th of September, 1993, and also signed by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. This is a similar document --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. There is a correction of the transcript. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some problem in the transcript. I believe that my colleague is referring to document D127 -- PDB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, this is evidently a letter that is very similar to the ones we have seen, but what I'm interested in here is that exchanges are mentioned here on the all-for-all principle, and this is obviously what the negotiations were based on. Please tell me: Were such exchanges agreed on, and was it possible to carry them out?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I proposed to the East Bosnia Corps and the Drina Corps that we carry out an all-encompassing exchange with the areas on the other side, that is, Tuzla and Zenica, that we carry out an all-for-all exchange, but before that, that we should all be quite sincere and open, and submit lists of all prisoners. All three corps worked on this, but unfortunately on that occasion we were unable to carry this out, for various reasons. In fact, Tuzla and Zenica were not able to establish a connection in some way. They had problems because they were not geographically close. They were cut off from each other. So that we had to carry out these exchanges in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber already knows this, but please tell us:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say Tuzla and Zenica, you're referring to a Muslim-controlled territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document mentions prisons in Banja Luka, in Tunjice, and the Batkovic collection centre. You see this in the third paragraph. At the time when this document was issued, were these the prisons controlled by the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. The word "VIZ" is mentioned here. This stands for military investigation institute in Banja Luka. The Tunjice prison is also in Banja Luka. It had been a prison before the war, a district prison, in fact, and the collection centre in Batkovic, near Bijeljina, was established in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D173/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My next question is: Within the 1st Krajina Corps, or rather, the territory covered by this corps, was there a military court, a military prosecutor's office, and military judicial organs competent for your corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were in Banja Luka, and we cooperated with them normally. There was no other way. The Court was staffed when military lawyers arrived from Zagreb, so that all the judicial organs were fully staffed within the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for someone to be exchanged if legal proceedings had been instituted against them, before the military judicial organs, without the approval of these organs or without your applying to these organs for approval? Was that possible, if you knew that proceedings had been instituted against someone?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I used to work in a penal institution, and all of us, even if we were civilians, were searched by the guards; and if we were allowed to enter, then we were let in; otherwise, no. The military judicial organs had their military police, and we were not able to take anyone out without approval. Of course, we didn't have the right to do this. We could only do what I have already described, and that is to ask for amnesty or pardon for that person, if this was in the interests of the exchange, but this would have to be issued by a higher organ, but no one could issue orders to the judiciary organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the East Bosnia Corps also had military judicial organs, a military court, and a military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the East Bosnia Corps, they had this also. We cooperated with them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another document I wish to be shown to the witness in connection with this topic is document PDB 105/3. It is a description -- or rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A letter of the 10th of May, 1993, addressed to the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you again, Mr. Grujicic: Is this your signature, and what can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature. I drew up this document. And prisoner Ivan Matkovic -- that is, everything that had to be done under the law had been done, and as he was in the military investigation detention unit, because they had room there, he was left there, even afterwards. We took him out for exchange with Vujadin Cecavac. They both hailed from the Odzak municipality but one was a Serbian, the other was a Croat. Mr. Vujadin Cecavac was exchanged for the second time because he had been taken prisoner twice. Since the exchange had been agreed with the HVO commission, we carried out this job successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Was this regular procedure? It says May 1993 here. Did you work the same way in 1992 in connection with prisoners that were under the jurisdiction of the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: From May 1992, this was the procedure that had been prescribed and according to which people worked. However, until May 1992, while the JNA still existed, we asked the federal secretariat for National Defence from Belgrade for approval, because we were within the JNA. This procedure was a bit more difficult, because it was a bit time-consuming, but we indeed managed to do it, and how. After all, the army was organised. It had these services, and therefore, that's the way things worked from day one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished with this document, thank you. And now I would like it to get a number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is numbered D174/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, tell us: What was the principle of people stating their actual views at the separation line where they were about to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: During 1991 and the beginning of 1992, while we did not have representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross, we, both commissions, that is, would hear, at the place of exchange, from all the people there as to who wanted to go for an exchange and who did not. Because, quite simply, from both sides there were people who didn't want to be exchanged, who wanted to go back to their families, and we would honour that. When the International Red Cross started to work in our area too, then the representative of the International Red Cross would get a list. If he boarded a Serb bus, then from the Serbs, from us, that is, and then he would call out the names of the Croats, who would say, loud and clear, whether they wanted to be exchanged or not. And the reverse was also true. When they would finish in one bus, then they would go to the other bus and do the same thing. So it was the free will of the prisoners that was the rule advocated by the representatives of the International Red Cross, and we accepted that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. We have an objection from the Prosecution, or perhaps it's not even an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's actually a clarification. Could we have some clarification of where exactly the witness is referring to and the period, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, perhaps you heard this. Perhaps you didn't. The objection of the Prosecution or, rather, their wish to have this clarified. When you're explaining this, which period does this refer to, this which you told us about, the procedure of people stating their own views?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: It pertains to the first exchanges that we carried out before the representatives of the International Red Cross came, as I already said. We together did this, both sides. We heard people's views. As soon as the representative of the International Red Cross came - and this was already in 1992 - I mean, in 1991, Mrs. Heidi Huber was there, and we did part of the work involved, but she was too far away, and she had to cover a very big area. I, for instance, have many letters in which we asked the representative of the International Red Cross to come and to do certain things. However, I assume the area was enormous, as I said. There was a war going on. It was not easy to come. So sometime from 1992, when the representative of the International Red Cross came to Banja Luka, Mr. Michel Janaret I don't know exactly how to pronounce this, because I don't speak English, then there weren't any problems involved any longer. On the other hand, the Tuzla region, for example, the HVO had its dealings with the International Red Cross in Osijek, and the Zenica region had a representative of the Red Cross in Zenica. So often we would have even two representatives of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, could you speak a bit slower so that all of this could be interpreted. Tell me now: These persons that you took for an exchange, these prisoners of war, before being taken for an exchange, they were in detention, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: After these persons would state their views at the exchange line, if a certain person did not want to go and be exchanged, was any person ever returned to detention?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, this is hard. I mean, I can tell you about our side, but I can't tell you about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please not speak at the same time as the witness, asks the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: As for those persons who stated their views, namely, that they wished to say, regardless of whether they were Serbs, Muslims or Croats -- of course, such a person would be allowed to do that. If this person had residence in Republika Srpska or in Western Slavonia, then this person would be allowed to return home. Because once these exchanges started, and once there was this procedure, there was nothing wrong with such a person. The anathema was no longer there, so this person would turn out to be a free person and could go wherever he or she wished to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to move on to a different topic now. Perhaps we could have a break now. I know that I have a bit more time left, two minutes, but perhaps this would be a convenient time to take a break, and perhaps it would be a good thing for the witness to get some rest as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can take our break and continue our proceedings at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we just have to wait a few -- yes, here he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're going to continue, Mr. Grujicic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat this? Can we hear each other?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I can hear you well. I assume that you can hear me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. Now we can hear you fine. Mr. Grujicic, my next question: When you negotiate and when you have exchanges with the other side, how did you communicate with the other side? Did you have direct contacts or did you have contacts through certain communications equipment? Was it the same always, throughout the period?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't. In 1991, when the war broke out, up until the month of November, we had telephone communications. That was the easiest way of reaching agreement. However, when there were certain disruptions, then these lines were cut off. So then we used the reporting centres attached to the military. And through these centres, for example, if we did not have such communication on the other side, then from these centres we would ask for ham radio operators to get in touch with this other state. So it would happen that, for example, if I needed to communicate specifically with Orasje, and if we could not establish it directly, then on one occasion we would get a ham radio operator from Pula, we would give him the telephone number of the gentleman from Orasje so that he could inform them that they should come to their centre so that we could reach agreement on a meeting, exchanges, or other things that we had to agree upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Later on, did these negotiations become direct? Did they become more frequent? Did you personally meet up with the representatives of the other side? And when did this start, if there were such negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear on this. Our commission had a large area to cover, and every day we went somewhere for negotiations, exchanges, or other things. If we are, for example, negotiating with Orasje, and if we know that perhaps we will not have an opportunity to talk to each other because we would be absent, then we would propose to the gentleman, for example, the following week, that same day, at the same time, at the same place, and this would remain as our agreement. So there were such ways as well. Very successfully so. As a matter of fact, we said every week, every -- the same day, the same time, the same place. And we indeed found this useful, because there were different problems. When we would succeed in having the commands set up telephones at positions between our unit and the enemy unit, the so-called hot lines, they would only be used by the commanders. If there were certain violations in terms of what had been agreed upon previously. However, if there had to be negotiations, then the commanders would not mind if we would, with their approval, use this telephone of theirs. So that was also one of the ways in which we communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Grujicic: We heard quite a few testimonies before this Court that there were frequent negotiations and exchanges between the side of Republika Srpska and the side of the HVO, that there were in the so-called UNPAs. In your work, you covered that region too, and you worked on negotiations in other areas that were not UN-protected areas. What were the advantages of the UNPAs, if any, in relation to negotiations that were held outside such areas, and exchanges themselves, of course?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: In this past war, Western Slavonia, where I come from too, was the first one to be handed over to the UN. The United Nations guaranteed the safety of the population in that area. That is where the United Nations forces came. They secured passages. No heavy weapons were allowed, only short-barreled weapons, whereas we negotiators, when we'd come from, say, Banja Luka, we would have to report everything, or rather, we would have to inform UNPROFOR, in the UNPA, that we were coming to negotiate with the opposite side. We would also have to inform the local police in the UNPA and the police in Republika Srpska, at the crossings where we would be going over to the other side. Everything had to be covered with permits and papers. In addition to that, for a while, or rather, most often, we could not cross over to the other side wearing uniform. This caused difficulties for me, because I had to change in the car in front of the bridge, and it was wintertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What was the situation like in the other places that were not UN-protected areas?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, then both sides would agree that the war would be stopped at the locality where negotiations were taking place, depending on how much time we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. When you say "two, three, five," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I mean they would stop for two, three, or five hours, depending on how much time we needed, depending on how much time we needed for negotiations. Then these approvals would be issued, although often there would be violations and our lives would be at risk. However, that is where we had all the representatives of the international institutions: UNPROFOR, the European Mission, the ICRC, all thee represent these representatives. And then, of course, we would protest if there had been a violation of that agreement of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell the Trial Chamber: Who did you negotiate with? What was the other entity that you were negotiating with in those territories that were not UN-protected areas?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, under UN protection, or rather, the Zenica district, the Tuzla district, and Orasje were not under UN protection. These are areas where the UN had not taken them over as their own areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the representatives of Orasje went for negotiations and exchanges with you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The representatives of Orasje would come to Dragalic most often. This is in Western Slavonia, in the UNPA zone. Or, if there was sudden gunfire there, we would go to Lipovica, but then we would have problems because we would have to ask for permission from the civil police, the military police, the Republic of Serbia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment, sir. You mentioned these approvals. We already have this in evidence. Who on behalf of the negotiators and those who went for exchange, who was it who obtained all these permits and approvals to move through the territory and enter the UNPA zone?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: In our area, it was I who did that, because I come from Western Slavonia, and of course I knew everyone. But regardless of personal contacts, what had to be covered by documents had to be covered by documents. When we went to Lipovica on the Republic of Serbia, then we would ask the gentleman from the East Bosnia Corps to do that, because this was closer to them and they did that more often, and they would get permission, and we would submit to them our list of people, or rather, of negotiators, people to be exchanged, and people we wanted to get in exchange. In Orasje, this was very convenient. In Dragalic, in the UNPA zone, it was quite far from us, but we had no other opportunities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said there were some incidents. Do you remember an incident that took place at Malinjak, near Lukovac, where members of the commission were shot at? Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I remember many events. For instance, let me describe one of these, near Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: We arrived for negotiations, and it was very risky. Moreover, most of the representatives of the Red Cross from our side and journalists turned back. But a member of the commission from Mrkonjic Grad, Mladen Arezina, I, and the military police and my driver, we went ahead, regardless of the danger. And in brief, when we found ourselves at the negotiations, everything proceeded as usual. But half an hour later, there was a rifle shot on one side, another one on the other side, and then the exchange became faster and faster, and they opened up fire. They fired on the school building, where we were. I don't believe they were aiming at us, but it was most unpleasant. And at one point, Mr. Meho Spriritovic from Jajce, asked me: Mr. Grujo, what shall we do now? And I said to him: Meho, we have to fly the flag of the Red Cross. So the two of us climbed up onto a high place in order to calm down the passions of war on both sides. He said to me: I dare not -- my sugar level will rise up to 300. So there was nothing for it but for my driver and I to go out. I used my megaphone, and because we were in a valley, I yelled at the top of my voice: Stop shooting. Excuse me. There are international negotiators here. Which wasn't true, but I used this little trick for the sake of both sides, because they would think, if the international community is here, they will register who started first, and then there will be discussion of this incident, and fortunately they did stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that this sort of situation occurred often. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You mentioned Malinjak. A rifle went off by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We won't go into this now.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Grujicic, tell me what I and this Court are most interested in, and that is: What was the relationship between the military and civilian commissions, and why did there have to be any sort of relationship between the military and civil commissions? What made them work together?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The unfortunate war. First there was the military commission, the geographic area was enormous, and of course we couldn't be everywhere at once. All the men were at the front line. Families had a difficult time. When they heard that their men were missing - I'm referring to the women - it was hard for them to reach us in Banja Luka because there was no traffic, and also it was quite risky and quite far. Then a part of this humanitarian activity which falls within the sphere of activity of the Red Cross was taken over by them, and the families would apply to them. In some municipalities which bordered on the front line, civilian commissions were set up. The commissions consisted of people who knew the people in their territory. They would establish telephone or fax connections with us and submit requests to us, because units were established according to municipalities. In this way, communication was faster, so that the missing, the imprisoned, and those killed could be reported faster. The civil commissions and the Red Cross were very important. We didn't have any authority over these commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go into that later.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, when was the first time you established contact with the Samac commission? Can you tell us when this was and when you got to know Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Through the media, we were informed, like everybody else, about what had happened in Odzak. The roads then were not open. It was not possible to travel to Yugoslavia. In the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, I assume an order was issued to break through and establish a corridor. I had never been in Samac before that time, nor did I know anyone there, but through the media I learnt of two men who were doing, as far as they were able, work on exchanges, and these were civilians who had not been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. We had some technical difficulties. You learned through the media of two men. Can you repeat what you said after that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I read the names of two men in the papers who were carrying on this humanitarian activity between the municipality of Samac and the opposite side, that is, the municipality of Odzak. These two men were Velimir Maslic and Miroslav Tadic. I had never seen those men, nor did I know them. When the corridor was opened up, I think it was in July 1992, though I'm not sure - I went there because the area of Samac municipality was also covered by our corps, and I knew about the prisoners in Odzak, so I went to link up with Miroslav Tadic and Veljo Maslic, to get to know them and to agree with them as to what should be done in future in order to free the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that when you got to know them?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: When I first arrived, I met Mr. Velimir Maslic. I got to know him then. But I didn't see Miroslav, because Mr. Maslic told me that Miroslav was away somewhere negotiating. I didn't know the area, but he was away, so I met him on my next visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, from the time you met them, did you begin working together? Did you go to negotiations together? Did you organise exchanges together, each doing their own part of the job?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: From that time, not only did we establish links with the municipality of Samac, but also with the municipality of Modrica, which is in the same area, and we hadn't had connections with it before. The municipality of Doboj was under the command of our corps. Then we agreed that it would be a good thing if they were also to attend the negotiations, so that they could discuss - I'm referring to the civilian commissions - so that they could talk the reuniting of families and the passage of civilians, while we, the military commission, held talks with the military commission on the other side about the exchange of prisoners. And that is how it was all the time. On both sides, we always had this composition of negotiating teams: Civilian commissions or, if there was no civilian commission, the Red Cross, plus the military commission. This was the team, the team doing humanist work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document PDB 63/3. This is a letter to the Ministry of Justice from the commission for exchanges, dated the 12th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you sign this document, and what can you tell us about it, Mr. Grujicic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I signed this document. Two days before I wrote this document, I was visited by a gentleman from the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska, from Pale, that is, Serbian Sarajevo, Mr. Slobodan Markovic. He introduced himself as a member of the republican commission. I explained the problems to him in connection with moving around on the ground. We, the military commission, received passes and permits from our command, and we were able to move around in the area covered by our command. Civilians had more problems than us, and when I explained this to him, he said: We will issue a single card, enabling people to move throughout the territory of Republika Srpska. Apart from the military commission, to submit to us also the names of the representatives of the civilian commission also. In this case, in Samac, the president was Mr. Velimir Maslic, and there was another one in Modrica and so on, so I submitted the names so that they could get these passes as soon as possible, and later on we got other passes as well, including one for Miroslav Tadic. On the basis of these passes, we could move around on the territory not only of the 1st Krajina Corps, but on the entire territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is D175/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another document on the topic you have talked about, that is, PDB 74/3. It is a letter to UNPROFOR, dated the 5th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have already told us that you wrote letters of approval, or rather, letters requesting approval of the appropriate institutions, and UNPROFOR and the police station of Stari Gradiska and Gradiska mentioned here. In the second paragraph here, there is mention of Veljo Maslic from Bosanski Samac. Are you the author of this document, and can you explain to us why a member of the civilian commission should be appointed as the person responsible for this exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I wrote this letter. I signed it in my own hand. And the answer to your question is the following: The year 1993 was a year when we had problems in connection with fuel. We agreed with the East Bosnia Corps that whatever we could do together, we would do, as regards paperwork, but to reduce our expenses, as the neighbouring municipality was Samac, I agreed with them that, let's say, the gentleman from Samac - sometimes it was Velimir Maslic; in this case it was he, and sometimes it was Mr. Miroslav Tadic - that they should go to the East Bosnia Corps to collect the prisoners to be exchanged. I appointed Veljo Maslic, the responsible person, for the passage through the area from the East Bosnia Corps to Gradiska, at the bridge, and then I would take over. Therefore, for the sake of savings and to reduce the amount of work, we divided the job in this way. The East Bosnia Corps knew that the gentleman from Samac, and sometimes from Modrica, could do this job, because we had already drawn up all the necessary documents beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now for something that I said that I would ask you about separately. The members of the civilian commissions, did they have any possibility to participate in the decision-making of the military commissions, and the other way around; did the military commissions take part in that? I mean, did they decide on structures and on exchanges, civilians for the military and the military for the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: We could only talk with the representatives of the civilian commissions. Before we would draw up a list for exchanges, in order for the prisoners who were from the area to be there, because when we from the commission would send the list to all those authorities that I mentioned already, and when we would get their consent, then I would be the person who would copy this list, in a verified fashion. I would sign it, and it was only in that form that the prisoners could be picked up from the prisons where they were, and then these people could come with me for the exchange. The civilian commissions did not interfere, but they were welcome. They had excellent cooperation with us. And of course, the army came from their localities, and therefore we cooperated. But I see this cooperation through the ICRC and other bodies. The representatives in the international community were often there. Most often it was the representatives of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please get a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D176/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown another document related to this subject, PDB 77/3. I shall call it the letter to Maslic, Velimir, dated the 13th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document is also self-explanatory. First I'll ask you whether you signed it, and what was the reason why you addressed the Samac commission, or rather, Mr. Maslic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am the person who signed this letter. Since we were involved in negotiations every day throughout our territory, we were divided up into several groups. We asked the gentleman from Samac, Mr. Veljo, to get in touch with Mr. Matija Bodirogic, who -- or rather, sorry, it was still Jovika Savic then, who was quite ill. He had diabetes. He died ultimately. So we were always together at negotiations and talks. And at one point, in a particular area, a certain group of Muslims was supposed to be exchanged, those who were in our prison. So we gave them to the East Bosnian Corps because they had been sought. The East Bosnian Corps agreed on the exchange of some combatants from our area too. However, this exchange failed. It did not come through. Therefore, I asked Veljo Maslic, president of the civilian commission, to contact -- or rather, I asked that he should check this with Jovika to see what should be done so that we should exchange these four names that are mentioned here. These are representatives of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, who were taken prisoner in Slunj. They were supposed to be exchanged in our area.
