So Veljo was asked for those reasons, because we were absent quite often, and sometimes our communications did not work properly but theirs did, so this was purely for technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question in relation to this document was whether Velimir Maslic or, rather, the civilian commission, in addition to conveying information, could they do anything in terms of decision-making in respect of these requests?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No. I've told you: Before a list would be compiled, then we could talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to go into all of this. It's all right. You've already explained this. I just asked you specifically, in addition to conveying this information, you asked me whether there was anything else and you said no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So then we don't have to go into that. You also said this person, Jovika -- you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: It was Major Jovika Savic, at that time president of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war of the East Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document number is D177/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Pera [as interpreted] Jakovljevic, and do you know what that person did, what line of work he was involved in?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Colonel Petar Jakovljevic, or Pero, is a person I only knew over the telephone. I did not know him personally. He was deputy commander for security at the East Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document 102/3. I'll call the document the letter to Pero Jakovljevic, dated the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, you are probably familiar with this document as well. Is this your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. My signature is on it, both. I know the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The letter is self-explanatory. We don't need details. But I would be interested especially in the following: I see from the first paragraph that you had had a telephone conversation previously, but you insist in this document that you get approval in writing. Now, my question is the following -- can we hear each other?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is whether it was necessary to get approval in writing with respect to the exchange of each and every prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: For every exchange, a written approval was required. This letter shows that we obtained the consent of the military prosecutor, and also Mr. Pero gave us his consent by telephone. However, on the basis of this consent, we also got approval from the Main Staff, and subsequently he called the Main Staff and said that he did not agree with this. Of course I was surprised to hear that. The army always asked for something to be done according to the rules of service. These are humanitarian matters. I observed the rules of service. But when a humanitarian matter is involved, some things can be skipped. So I felt that this was a question of this officer's vanity. Perhaps he looked down on me because I was a reservist. So that is why I was sharp with regard to this matter, because I got all the approvals required. I called him yet again by telephone, and ultimately he was told by the Main Staff that he should not create any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please get a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D178/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document was internally marked PDB 106/3. I shall call it the invitation to attend a meeting, dated the 11th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, you've probably signed this document too. Tell us: What was the reason for writing this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I received an order from the president of the republican commission, Captain Dragan Bulajic, to convene a meeting in our area, that is to say, in the Banja Luka region, in the Krajina region, and to invite all the representatives of the military commission and the civilian commissions, and the Red Cross too. I wrote down these telephone numbers here because there was no other way. It was urgent. And then I asked for all these people to be informed, because this had to do with reaching agreement on a larger, more comprehensive exchange. And in order to have something like that done, all the participants had to be there. When we did not have somebody's telephone number, for example, Miroslav Tadic, then we actually had the telephone of the Red Cross. I mean, he did not have a telephone then, or whatever. So the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: Were such meetings often organised, those that were sought by the state commission, and were the local commissions present, or was this a rare case of such meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: This was one of the rare meetings of this kind. The war zone of the 1st Krajina Corps, we had more -- meetings more often, because we often had negotiations. For example, if we were to be in Gradacac one day for negotiations, when we would go to -- back to Modrica, we would first analyse what we had done and then we would agree on the next exchange, and that's the way it was, wherever we happened to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you had these meetings, these internal meetings of yours, if I can put it that way, at the level of the corps, were these meetings often attended by the representatives of the civilian commissions with regard to the organisation of following exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: It wasn't often the case; it was always the case. In order to be as successful as possible - I've already said that we would go together to no man's land, and everybody would negotiate with their representative at that particular point. So it was quite compulsory. It was natural for all of us to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said: So it was quite compulsory, and then we lost contact. What were the words you said after that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I said it was compulsory, and I said it was natural for all of us to meet up on the actual spot. I can only add one more thing: If there was a little problem, if I can express myself that way, not a real problem but sort of a little problem in the negotiations, then they would call me and the representative of the military commission from the other side, so that we would agree together. We would not resolve the dispute. I mean, we would simply agree, discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to ask for a number for this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D179/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you first started speaking, when we looked at the decision appointing you president of the commission for exchanges of the 1st Krajina Corps, we said that there were military representatives there at first, but later on did it happen that your commission got more members? And I would like to ask the registrar to prepare the document P109/3, to be shown to the -- I'm sorry. I have to correct myself. This is an internally marked document, PDB 109/3. I just said "P." I'm sorry. Could you please tell us about this document. This is a document that I will denote as order of the first KK, dated the 18th of May, 1993. What is different here in relation to the previous decision that we've already tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I've said to you that the general ordered me to write for him what my view was as to what the commission should look like. When I wrote that, he said to me that I should propose people for that. I did not know about that, but in various ways I did get people's names and I did make such a proposal. I became member of that commission, and my profession is teacher. Lieutenant Colonel Uros Mirosljevic, he was representative of the security of our corps. Malic, Dusan, he was in Derventa, a teacher from there, in charge of the area of Derventa, Brod, and Odzak, so that was closest to him. Arezina, Mladen, was an economist from Mrkonjic grad and he was in charge of the following municipalities: Sipovo, Donji Vakuf, and Jajce. Branislav Urosevic, reserve Captain First Class from Doboj, member of the military commission, in charge of Doboj, Teslic, and Modrica. Radoljub Trkulja a veterinarian, also from Mrkonjic Grad, in charge of Jajce and Skender Vakuf. He was a younger man, very pedantic and very courageous in our activities. Milan Bobic was my driver or -- I mean, sorry, the commission's driver, and then there was also security. Miroslavka Jokanovic, who we also exchanged from Travnik, she was the person who listed all the exchange persons in the computer, and Mrs. Biljana Culum, she was a lawyer and she was secretary of the commission. Well, that's it. That's the new commission that could normally carry out all its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Grujicic. I will have to ask you to speak a bit slower, once again. I'm going to read these names now and you tell me if I read them out right. Just say yes or no. Number 1, Milutin Grujicic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 2, Uros Mirosljevic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 3, Malic, Dusan?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 4, Arezina, Mladen?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 5, Branislav Urosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 6, Rodoljub Trkulja?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Trkulja, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 7, Milan Bulovic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 8, Miroslavka Jokanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 9, Culum, Biljana?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please: In the introductory part, it says that one of the tasks of the commission will be to assist in organising the exchange of civilians and of art objects and sacred objects.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: In connection with civilians, that was put in because in our title there was a part referring to families of soldiers who had crossed over from the other side, and they were afraid for their families, so they asked for their families to be brought over so they could be reunited. As for objects of art and ecclesiastical objects, yes, because every nation has its own history and heritage, and we didn't want this to be destroyed. So if there was any possibility, that we should do this. This was a case in Travnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We won't go into details.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, the last sentence, the translation is a bit awkward. It says to the assistant commander for UNPROFOR. Can you explain whether this assistant commander was attached to your command, whether he was in charge of cooperation with UNPROFOR and civilian affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: There's something missing here. The commission is subordinate to the assistant commander for cooperation with UNPROFOR and civilian affairs, so he was the assistant of General Talic. It's a bit awkward here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document number is D180/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, we have heard testimony here about Batkovic, and I will ask you whether you know, in view of the fact that you covered an area that did not include the Batkovic camp, do you know, in view of your cooperation and correspondence with the East Bosnia Corps, what was the procedure to get a person out of Batkovic and be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Of course, I know about the procedure, yes, just as was the case with us in Banja Luka. The gentleman from the East Bosnia Corps, if we agreed to have certain persons exchanged, they would have to get all the approvals and permissions from the judiciary, from the corps security organs and from the Main Staff. When all this had been obtained on the day the exchange was to take place, they could take out the persons to be exchanged. There was no other way. The persons who were to be exchanged could be collected by the person mentioned in the order. Very often it happened, or it would happen sometimes, that, along with the presence of the East Bosnia Commission, either Velimir Maslic or Miroslav Tadic went to collect the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you yourself wrote to the East Bosnia Corps, saying that Miroslav Tadic would come to collect the prisoners? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I did write, and this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your cooperation with Miroslav Tadic like, in general? I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the period when you cooperated with the Samac commission, what was your cooperation with Mr. Miroslav Tadic like? Was he different from the other people you cooperated with in the civilian commissions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Our cooperation - I'm referring to the military commission - both with Velimir Maslic and Miroslav Tadic, was correct and successful. How could it have been otherwise? Miroslav Tadic is a humane person. He's a person who wished to help those who needed help the most, in wartime. Never did I receive any complaints at any of the negotiations from anyone on the opposite side in connection with any of the people in the delegation, including the military commission, the civilian commission, and the representatives of the Red Cross. We always did our best to have things done in a fair and correct manner. I think the gentlemen from Samac, Velimir Maslic and Miroslav Tadic, were selfless in carrying out their tasks. Moreover, Miroslav Tadic, on one occasion, paid for fuel for the transport of prisoners out of his own pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown document PDB 118/3. This is a letter to the ICRC, dated the 17th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are probably the author of this document also. Can you tell us the reason for the writing of this letter and what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I signed this letter, and I also wrote it to the representative of the ICRC in order to inform him and to have him present at the negotiations that were to be held in the area of Pakrac. Mr. Michel however, did not attend these negotiations, because at these negotiations, almost all the Croatian and Serbian commissions were present. The negotiations were chaired by the chief of the International Committee of the Red Cross. I apologise. I don't speak English, but I think his name was Ponfly [phoen] and he was the chief from Zagreb. He was the one who chaired the meeting which was held -- which lasted from 10.00 a.m. to 8.00 p.m. It went on for about ten hours. And we were quite successful at the level of the entire Serbian and Croatian area. After the meeting, of course we went on to agree on those obligations that we had undertaken, and I assume the Croats did the same. So that was the meeting in Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, in general, what was your relationship with the International Red Cross in connection with the work you were doing? Did you have any complaints from that institution on your work or the work of people who you were associated with?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any problems, because these were people who came to help us. In that evil time, through them - and this refers to all sides - we tried to find out about prisoners whom we assumed had been taken prisoner, but we had not received a positive reply from the other side. We asked the representatives of the ICRC to check whether the other side was holding people whose names we had listed. We received a lot of help from them. We cooperated very well, and I have to say that they were happy with our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally receive an invitation from the ICRC to visit Geneva? Who did you get it from, and what was it about?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I had a very good cooperation with Mr. Michel who was the representative of the ICRC in Banja Luka. He was a man with a great deal of experience in that sort of work, worldwide. He had been in other parts of the world before. He was young. He wanted to do his job even when his own vehicle was shot at. When he left Banja Luka, a meeting was held in Geneva of representatives of the Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, and he, of course, expected me to be there at that meeting, and he came to look for me there, but there were other people, so he sent his regards. I wish I could send him my regards as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number for this document is D181/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, I will put a few questions to you concerning two specific exchanges, about which we have heard testimony at this Tribunal, and the facts you know in connection with these exchanges. And we can see from the documents that you know a lot about many exchanges, but now I will ask you about two specific exchanges and certain facts connected with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown document PDB 117/3. The document is a letter to the chief of the Samac public security station, Stevan Todorovic, dated the 17th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document and then tell me what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: We had agreed on an exchange with the HVO, which was to take place on the 15th of June, 1993, and on this occasion, in agreement with the Bijeljina Corps, I had agreed that Mr. Miroslav Tadic should go to collect the prisoners. So he was just going to collect them. Miroslav Tadic did that job well, but something unexpected happened. The fuel ran out and he was unable to obtain any. We had agreed that the exchange would take place in Dragalic at 11.00. The Croatian side, however, and the HVO, and we, waited and waited. On that spot, we had no telephone lines, so I asked the gentleman from the HVO to wait and I would go back to Bosanska Gradiska, with my driver, and try to telephone, in order to find out what was going on. I called our command, our military command, and I asked them to go and check. Miroslav came back there and he explained to me that there was a problem with fuel. It was already 1800 hours, so there had been a delay from 1100 to 1800 hours, and he suggested that he hand over the prisoners to the police station, the public security station in Samac, and during the night he would try to solve the problem -- besides this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. We had some technical problems. The last thing we heard was "during the night." Can you repeat what you said after that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: During the night he would try to solve the problem of petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I promised that I would call the command in Modrica, if necessary, but Miroslav, as usual, solved the problem successfully, and on the following day -- during the night he let them know that he could bring the people at 8.00 a.m., if necessary. But I came back on that day. I went back to Dragalic and I told the gentleman from the HVO, after apologising, I told them what had happened and we agreed to meet at the same place, the same time, on the following day. And I told Miroslav to bring the prisoners to Dragalic at 11.00 a.m. We met him in Bosanska Gradiska, took over command of everything, and set out to the negotiations and exchange. Because let's understand each other: Whenever there was an exchange, we also conducted negotiations. We would analyse what had been done and put forward proposals for the next exchange. When we arrived at the motorway near Dragalic, I went to tell the representatives of the HVO that everything was all right, that all the people on the list were there, and that the exchange could begin. However, at one point Miroslav approached me and said that certain problems had arisen. What was the problem? He said that prisoners had been beaten up in the Samac public security station. I simply couldn't believe it, because I exerted influence on all the members of all the commissions to ensure that in their areas they would to their utmost to prevent such unfortunate incidents. But now I myself, I found myself in an embarrassing situation. I think the prisoner's name was Salkic, I think, and he showed me and Miroslav, and also the representatives of the international community and the representatives of Croatia, what had happened. I was horrified. I apologised to the HVO commission and I said that I would do everything in my power, that I would inform my command, and that I was sure that my command would help us and issue an order that something like this should never happen again. After I heard from Miroslav Tadic that the chief was Stevan Todorovic - I didn't know him, but I consider him to be responsible - I wrote this letter right away, in order to inform him of this and to tell him that something like this must never happen again. I also informed our commander, General Talic, and he issued an order that all prisoners had to be kept safe, that they could be questioned but not beaten, if they were going to be exchanged [as interpreted]. Miroslav Tadic again carried out a humane job. There was no conflict. And why? Because we were all amazed when we saw the corpus delicti and all we could do was apologise to the other side and then agree on further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I have an intervention in respect of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Interpretation, because -- actually, this is not what the witness said, here on page 59, lines 17 and 18. It seems that, according to what is in transcript - and this is not what I heard from the witness - that the only -- those who are going to be exchanged were not supposed to be beaten. So maybe this can be clarified. This is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think counsel should clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, we have a small problem with the transcript. I will have to ask you again to speak a bit slower, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the beatings, did you mean the beatings of only those who were supposed to be exchanged, or did you mean beatings in general in prisons that were under the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I said that there was an order that prisoners, when they were being taken prisoner, had to be handed over in the same condition in which they were when they had been taken prisoner, that they should not be beaten, and that means that from that moment until the exchange, they were not allowed to be beaten. These were incidents that occurred at given points in time. This happened on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, in relation to these incidents that occurred: What about you, the people who worked on exchanges? Did this work well for you, that such incidents would take place in respect of the work you did?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: This indeed made our work far more difficult. First of all, we, as humanists -- I mean, I, as a teacher, never slapped a pupil or caned a pupil. I thought that my word should be the strongest and that it is my word that would work far more efficiently than any beating. So in these situations, we also agreed that this should not be allowed to happen. It would slow things down. There could be retaliation. There could be beatings on the other side, without giving thought to it. This is wartime; it's not peacetime. And then it made things more difficult for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did these incidents decrease the confidence that had been established between the negotiators? Could they affect the trust that had been established during the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No, for a simple reason: Because I always knew that neither the opposite side nor us were in favour of such dirty things, and I mean we never had the opportunity of doing any such thing. How could I go to prisons and beat people up if my job was something quite different? So we trusted one another, because we knew that this part of the work probably took place where there were either civilian or military policemen, so it could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document number is D182/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another exchange that I would like to discuss with you is something that again has to do with the facts that you know about. This is the exchange dated December 1993, on the occasion of the Catholic Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the exchange and what happened in Dragalic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. We called that the Christmas exchange. But could I please have the relevant paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have the document that has to do with that. We don't have that list of exchanges. But I can remind you that this was an exchange where civilians from Samac were exchanged for Christmas 1993, and there were Muslims and Croats involved.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: The gentlemen from the HVO -- I mean, these talks were often attended by Mr. Marko Milos from the Croatian side, and gentlemen from Samac, for the most part, did their part of the job very well, what they were in charge of. At one moment, when this exchange was discussed, Mr. Marko Milos said the following: Gentlemen, if possible, can the Croats celebrate mass --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what Mr. Milos said? And I'm going to ask you about this talk. When did it take place before the actual exchange? How many days before that, if you know the date, since if the exchange took place on Christmas day, Catholic Christmas, then when did the talks take place, and what did Mr. Milos say?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: If I were to look at my diary - I mean, I kept a diary throughout the war, every single day - then I could give you the exact date. But it was certainly about ten days before, because such a big group of civilians could not be transferred just like that. The commission from Samac would have to do a great many things, because many of these civilians reported to them at the Red Cross, where their office was, saying that they wanted to go over to the other side, since, for the most part, the younger men were on the other side. Then, in these talks, after we had finished with all military negotiations, then these negotiations started. At one point Marko Milos said: Gentlemen, if at all possible, let the Croat gentlemen from the area of Samac celebrate mass on their own land. And of course, in an informal conversation, he said to me: If help is required, please help them as much as possible. The gentlemen, even without my help, Maslic Velimir and Miroslav Tadic, carried out all the preparations for that day, that is, the 24th of December, 1993. There was a bit of a delay, so they came later. And from 6.00 p.m., which had been the agreed time, I think -- I mean, the weather was very bad on that day. It was raining, it was windy, so it was cold. All of us from our side met at the point by the Dragalic gasoline station -- excuse me - where the Nepalese battalion was. However, nobody showed up from the other side. Time went by. I was a bit confused by that. I tried to do something through the Nepalese battalion, but unfortunately we didn't manage to understand each other. There was a change in the Nepalese battalion. Those who had been there for six months had left, and new ones had just arrived, so we didn't really know each other yet. So we were waiting there until about 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening, and when we realised that there was no one from the other side, then I proposed to the gentlemen who had come to the point and who were supposed to cross over to Croatia that they should be patient. Because, you know what it's like. People came. There was no one from the other side. And all of this looked strange to them. I asked them to be patient. I said that Mr. Miroslav Tadic, Veljo Maslic, and I would go to Bosanska Gradiska and that we would try to get in touch with the Croatian commission one way or the other. However, we did not succeed to speak either to Mijo Matanovic or to Marko Milos, although we did have their telephones, although we called them through ham radio operators. Quite simply, there was something suspicious as to what was going on. Later on, I heard that they had had information stating that only Muslims were being brought to them for an exchange, which was not true. While we were waiting and trying, all of a sudden a car appeared, an UNPROFOR car, the representatives of the Nepalese battalion. They came to my apartment where I was staying temporarily and they said that a representative of the Croatian side had come. It was Mr. Berislav Stetic, whom I knew well. He was a good co-worker of ours from Nova Gradiska. And then, when they informed us about this, we immediately set out yet again to the point in Dragalic. We came there. Of course, we found the gentleman concerned, and this is what he said to me: Mr. Grujicic, I did not come here to negotiate or to take over anyone, but I know how responsible you are. I know that this will cause problems, and if there's anything I can do to help, I'll try to do that. I said to him: Please, find, one way or the other, Marko Milos. Because, actually, in that situation he was the only one who could find a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We are going to pause here, and then after the break you will tell us how this ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that we could take the break now and have a break in the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please, and we'll have a break, but do instruct your witness to avoid unnecessary details, so that we can move on. We'll take a break for 20 minutes and resume at 12.50 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will continue, and I plan to finish my examination-in-chief very soon. But there is a question I have to put to the Prosecution. I have just found two pages of a text in English on my desk, mentioning Milutin Grujicic's name. I don't know whether the OTP wishes to use this document, which is a draft translation, to put some questions in cross-examination. If they do, I insist that the B/C/S version of this document be delivered to me and that my co-counsel in Belgrade be allowed - this is an unknown document. This is what the practice has been up to now, so that we can prepare, in order to be fair to the witness. Does the Prosecution intend to put any questions in cross-examination based on this document or, rather, this translation? It's a draft translation, and there is no B/C/S version. This is a transcript of a radio broadcast, apparently, but I know nothing about it. I've just found it on my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object strongly to what my learned friend has just said in front of the witness. Can the witness please be turned off so that I can respond to this? I provided my learned friends, out of courtesy, with the document, which I may use in cross-examination. If I can respond to this, I will do so, without the witness being turned on. It is most improper to reveal the contents of a document which may be used in cross-examination to a witness who is listening. It is something that should be spoken of out of court, or a ruling sought, in the absence of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are having problems with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are not receiving translation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The B/C/S booth notes that they cannot hear the proceedings from the courtroom. They have technical problems, says the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We seem to have problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't get an interpretation of what our learned friend has said, but I did understand. Your Honours, throughout these proceedings, any document that was put to a witness during cross-examination, when we were doing the cross-examination, had to be disclosed in time to the OTP. Let me remind you that on several occasions there was a break in the proceedings, so that the other side could prepare. I don't know what document this is. We need not discuss it before the witness. That wasn't my intention. It's simply that if this is a document that the OTP wishes to use during their cross-examination, the document should be handed to my co-counsel so that we can prepare. We have never yet had a situation where the OTP put a document on our desk without our being able to discuss the document with the witness. This is an example of hide and seek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Without disclosing the contents, what is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not saying while the witness is listening, Your Honour. I could have dealt with this -- Mr. Lukic could have spoken to me. I spoke to the other counsel. He could have spoken to me instead of raising it when you walked on the Bench instead of raising it with the witness. Now, I will deal with the issue, but not in front of the witness. It has nothing to do with preparing for the witness. It's something which, out of courtesy, a document I have given to the other counsel which I have discovered. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It does, but I'm not proposing to put the document into evidence. My learned friend could have found that out very easily by walking over and speaking to me rather than raising it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go ahead. The Prosecution have said that they're not proposing to use it to put the document in evidence. So go ahead. Because we have very limited time with videolink, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that doesn't -- I've given them a document which I may use the contents of, but it's not a document which I intend to put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you discuss that after we're through?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then see if you can come to an agreement, and the Trial Chamber will decide. Just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to burden the Chamber with this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, to put things briefly, I only wish you to tell us whether Mr. Milos, or rather, the representatives of the opposite side, arrived. If they arrived, when they arrived and what happened then? Was anything talked about with the persons to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I understand you. At about 1.00 a.m., Marko Milos arrived, with buses. He got permission from the deputy Prime Minister of Croatia, Mr. Kostovic, so that what had been agreed on could be carried out. And before I let Marko get into the bus and tell the truth to the people from the area of Samac, Marko got into the bus and said: Gentlemen, we apologise for this incident. Marko apologised. It is our fault. The Serbs did what we asked them to do. We had some misinformation on our side, among ourselves, and the Serbs have nothing to do with this problem. I apologise to you. The transfer of civilians from the buses which arrived from Samac, two buses brought by Mr. Marko Milos, started, and at around 3.00 a.m., that job was done. We said goodbye and went back, each to our own side, because on the following day there was to be an exchange and negotiations in Gradacac. We didn't get any sleep that night at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Grujicic, I will now move on to my final topic. You testified that during the exchanges you cooperated with a lot of people on both sides, on your own side and the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document PDB 131/3, and this is an excerpt from a newspaper, Krajski Vojnik [phoen] of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me in a few words why this article was written and whether it mentions all the people you were cooperating with at the time in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Every year --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please wait a little, and can you start again, because your answer wasn't recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Every year we conducted a review of the results of our work, so that on the basis of this, we could set our goals for the following year. This means that, in view of the corps command and the civilian organs, we were accountable to them for our work in the past year or, as in this case, the past two years. We did this, and the meeting was of course attended by all the representatives of the military commission, all the representatives of the civilian commission, the representatives of the Red Cross, the representatives of the ICRC, the European Mission, and other structures of the international community who were in this area. I mentioned here in the last part of this paragraph all the people who in various ways participated in this activity. Some of the former prisoners came to speak about their experiences before this gathering. General Talic, the commander, said that the results of the commission were indubitable. Work was conducted under difficult conditions. The lives of the members of the condition [as interpreted] were just as much at risk as the lives of the soldiers at the front line. Never before had so many living and dead soldiers been exchanged, because usually exchanges were carried out after wars ended. This means --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The Chamber will certainly be very interested in reading this whole article, but my question, since a large number of people are listed here, including the name of my client, Mr. Tadic, tell us whether you think that - and I'm here referring both to the military and the civilian commissions you cooperated with - whether you think that you were doing a humane job or a political job.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: This part of the work, had we obeyed the politicians, never would such a large number of people have been exchanged on our own initiative. We did something that was very difficult, that is, the exchange of prisoners of war. When listing these names, including Mr. Miroslav Tadic, I considered all of them to be humanists fighting for human lives. This article is written by a Muslim journalist named Dizdar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, I didn't ask you at the beginning of my examination, but could you now tell the Chamber where you are living now.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I am a refugee from the Republic of Croatia. My town is unfortunately no longer my town. I became a refugee on the 2nd of May, 1995, with my wife, and my mother remained at home. Later on I exchanged the house, and my mother, who was in prison for seven days - and she was 86 years old - I exchanged her as well, and she was the 12.001st person I exchanged in the municipality of Apatin [phoen]. We sold our house and we bought a flat in Sombor. I now live in Sombor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You probably wanted to say what you were doing now. Can you tell the Chamber where Sombor is, what country it's in?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where is Sombor? In which country?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Sombor is in Serbia, in the autonomous province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document number is D183/3 and ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, in your work, you evidently often met Mr. Tadic. In all your work, did you ever hear any complaints, by anyone, either in the commissions or from the people being exchanged, any complaints against his work?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: During the war, I often met, worked with, and reached agreements with Mr. Miroslav Tadic, among others, and I never heard any complaints from anyone. Had something happened, I would have been the first to object, because in our activity, 24 hours in a day were not enough. Even when we were asleep, we were thinking about prisoners and those who needed our help. This is the kind of thing Miroslav Tadic was a part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have already answered my next question, but please be very specific. Did you personally notice, in any action on the part of Miroslav Tadic, any kind of intolerance towards members of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Humanists cannot be intolerant. We tried to exchange or to have civilian commissions, allow passage of one ethnic group to their mother country, and had Miroslav Tadic been hostile in any way to members of other ethnic groups, his daughter would not have married a Croat. Besides this, Miro Tadic, whenever we met representatives from Orasje, was friendly. They would ask each other about all sorts of people whom they both knew. Mr. Mijo Matanovic comes from Odzak, and he knew Miroslav Tadic very well. I never received any kind of complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Grujicic: After these ten or more years, during which you worked on exchanges, do you feel that you were successful in this job?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. I think we have not successfully completed the job, because 24.000 persons are still missing, and this refers to all three ethnic groups: Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. In order to complete this job, because I could not rest in peace while this was still undone, I wrote to Gordon Bacon, who at that time was at the head of some sort of international Exchange Commission. I wrote to the commission of Republika Srpska, to the Yugoslav commission. I asked that they try, through the international community, to reactivate us, because we still had some knowledge among us that would certainly help a great deal to solve many cases of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel who wishes to ask questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Grujicic. I am Igor Pantelic and I defend Blagoje Simic from Samac. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I just have a few questions. In your work, since you have invaluable experience that you gained over all these years, do you have any personal knowledge? Were you, in a way, a witness as to whether Dr. Blagoje Simic took part in the work of your commission in any way? Did he exert any pressure? Did he exercise any influence in terms of whether somebody would be exchanged or not? What is your personal knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Throughout this period, I got to know Mr. Velimir Maslic and Mr. Miroslav Tadic from Samac quite well. That was sufficient for me in order to engage in the activities that were joint activities. As for Mr. Blagoje Simic, I do not know him personally, and I did not hear any complaints in terms of him influencing in any way the activities carried out by Miroslav Tadic and Velimir Maslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We don't intend to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, my name is David Re. I'm going to ask you some questions from the Prosecution. Can you hear me clearly, and do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I can hear you and I can understand you through the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you also see me on the screen while I'm asking you the questions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that I see you the way you see me, so I think we see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence has been of your commission working with the civilian commission for the exchange of prisoners and prisoners of war. What I want to ask you about is your experience or your involvement in Bosanski Samac and the exchanges there. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I understand. A civilian commission worked with us, and it is quite certain that we cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You cooperated because you had to coordinate your activities, such as making sure you each had lists and the right people at the exchange places at the right time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: That's right. It is certain that both sides, as I've already said, had its own lists, and in order to compile them, a broad number of activists is required for compiling that list, and then the list would go into the procedure that was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the success of each of these exchanges depended upon the closest cooperation between the civilian and military authorities, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the rules governing the exchange of prisoners of war and civilians were interchangeable, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you meant, but I don't really think so, because as far as prisoners of war were concerned, it was well known in which way they would be exchanged. As for civilian persons, through the corridors that had been established and agreed upon between the two sides, they would pass through them, and in this way, families would be reunited. So there is a difference, isn't there? We are intermediaries, because as the military commission, we secured passage through this corridor. This was a war -- or negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the middle part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We just lost the last part of your answer, Mr. Grujicic. We got up to "this was a war," and then we lost what you were saying. Could you just repeat that last part, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: This was a war, so it was impossible to go through positions any way people wanted. Movement was exclusively possible through corridors which we secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The army of the Republika Srpska operated -- or had a set of rules, didn't it, for the exchange of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did each corps have its own rules or did you operate according to the same rules?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that. I know about the East Bosnian Corps and I know about our corps. It was the East Bosnian Corps that first made their rules, and then we adjusted them to our own mode of work and to the ground in which the -- the area in which we operated. I assume that others did something along those lines too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Some of the exchanges that occurred were mixed exchanges, that is, there were civilians and prisoners of war being exchanged in the same exchange, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No. I said a while ago that by the time we would carry out the exchange of military prisoners, by then, the civilian commissions would deal with the civilian population. If it would so happen that there were civilian persons also on the list of the military commission, that was only for the sake of having safer passage through the military positions. Because during each and every passage, the military police or the unit at that position would check all the persons who were crossing over to no man's land.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Even if it were for safety reasons, what you're telling us now is that in some of the exchanges there were civilians who were included on the military list, and they went to the exchange at the same time as the prisoners of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I think that we simply haven't understood each other. I said that along with the soldiers who were going to be exchanged, we would put on the same list, in order to make passage easier through the front line and through the firing positions, we would do that. But in the place where the exchange would actually take place, then we would carry out a certain procedure in terms of the exchange of military prisoners. So a commission would establish -- would deal with them. The ICRC would ask them whether they wanted to go or not. As for civilians, they were free to go. They were free to pass over to one side or to the other side. So that's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But the names were on the same list as the POWs; is that what you're saying? I'm just trying to work that out.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in those circumstances, the ones you've just told us, where there was a mixture of names on the list, not on the exchange, but on the list, the exchange would be soldier for soldier, woman for woman, and elderly person for elderly person, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was for the most part, because I just know, when you say "woman for woman," I mean, I just know that we, for example, had a tank crew that were of the female gender only. So that sentence can be valid if there are prisoners that are taken. But it could have happened that a woman or an elderly person could have been involved, and when I say "elderly person," I mean military conscripts up to the age of 60 and reserve officers up to the age of 65 who do have military obligation and who either did certain work within their own local commune or, for example, they were in a fire-fighting unit or in a first aid unit. Such persons could have been taken prisoner too, and of course we would then pursue such activities as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The basis of the exchanges was on a one-for-one basis, wasn't it, one prisoner for another prisoner, one soldier for another soldier, one woman for another woman, one elderly person for another elderly person?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: That's not the way it always was. I'm talking about combatants, you know. A soldier is someone who exists in peacetime, but combatants exist in times of war. So that was the approach for combatants. However, when dead combatants were concerned, then this was not abided by, in order to honour the dead. We would deliver all the dead to the other side, irrespective of the numbers involved. As regards civilians who had certain obligations, then, irrespective of their number, they could pass freely. So the one-for-one principle was not applicable, because that is not an exchange. We had students going through as well. We asked for it, as a matter of fact. Students who happened to be on one side or another side. Then also high school students, then also from hospitals we had retarded persons, for example. We handled that too. Perhaps you could say exchange for that too, but that was not an exchange. It was help that was given to families who were looking for their nearest and dearest, and we did that with a lot of confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was only asking you about names on a list, Mr. Grujicic. I just want you to concentrate on that, please. The principle of putting names on a list for an exchange was that one side would compile a list of names and the other side would compile a list of the same number of names, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: No. No, sir. On a list, there could have been many more, and on another list there could have been far less. But as far as soldiers are concerned, then sometimes it would not be exactly one for one, even situations like that could happen. But as far as the passage of civilians is concerned, as I said, it depended on how many people they would take in in order to have families reunited. So it wasn't the principle of equal numbers that was applied there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In exchanging soldiers, there would be no reason -- or there was no reason to exchange a male soldier for a male soldier and a female soldier for a female soldier. A soldier was just a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: A soldier is a soldier, yes. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the practice was to ignore gender and, if your side had a soldier in custody, regardless of whether they're male or female, and the other side, the HVO, had a soldier, male or female, you exchanged the person, regardless of their gender; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Well, now, it's hard to be specific, for the simple reason that whether it was a woman for a woman, it's simply hard to answer that. I don't think that's so important. What really matters is -- both sides were happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just stop you there. We just missed part of your last answer. We got to "what really matters is," and we missed a part because of a technical breakdown. Can you just repeat that. "What really matters is" something, something, something, "both sides were happy to do it."

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: What was important was -- or rather, we did what was important. We didn't have many women in such situations. These were rare cases, and we did our work with full responsibility, bearing in mind that women especially had to be helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that the other corps adopted the East Bosnia rules and regulations -- East Bosnia Corps rules and regulations in relation to the exchange of prisoners of war. Now, those rules and regulations say - this is paragraph 13: "The exchange of prisoners of war shall be conducted on the one-for-one basis (soldier for soldier, woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person) or on the all-for-all basis." You told us a moment ago that these were the rules which you used. When these rules referred to soldier for soldier, woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person; you said woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person was to encompass those situations where there were names on the list which included civilians and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you stop there? I'm not saying that's what you said. You said you used those rules. I'm suggesting to you that that's what they mean, and I want you to comment on that. I'm suggesting to you that they -- the words "woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person" are inserted there to encompass situations when there was mixed civilians and prisoners of war on the list, not on the exchange but on the list. Sir, can you please confine it just to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If an article from this document is being put to the witness, the title of the document should be mentioned to the witness. The Prosecutor is basing his conclusion on part of the document, and he should put the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly have no objection to showing it to the witness, but I thought the witness understood clearly what I was saying to him. But if it will assist, I'll ask that P92/3 ter be placed on the ELMO, the page which has paragraph XIII on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the witness has already said he knows the document which I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only asked that when the article be quoted, that the title of the document be mentioned to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, I was reading from -- Article 13 will be placed on the monitor for you. The full title of the document is "Command of the East Bosnia Corps, confidential, 1/1369 to 2261, 7th of March, 1993, military secret confidential, pursuant to Article 175 of the law of the army of Republika Srpska and Article 3 of the provisional rules of service of the army of Republika Srpska. I hereby approve the following: Rules and regulations for the work of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war in the zone of responsibility of the IB corps to come into force on the 10th of March, 1993, signed Commander Colonel Novica Simic," signed and stamped. Are you clear that that's the document I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The wrong document was put on the ELMO, but what my learned friend has read is correct. That's what I wanted to have read. But the document is a completely different document, so let's not confuse the witness with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That was my fault. It was -- I was reading from the PDB number. It's D166/3. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the document, Mr. Grujicic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: It would have to be a little sharper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see it now, Mr. Grujicic? Can you see it clearly?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to read paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to read paragraph 13. That's the one I just read to you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, throughout my examination-in-chief we had a problem. The document would be put on the ELMO for only 10 to 15 seconds and then the image from the courtroom would come back. I have no objection to the Prosecutor reading the paragraph to the witness. What was important for me was to have the witness hear the title of the document, the full title of the document as it stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Grujicic, do you know what I'm referring to? It's Article 13, which was placed on the screen for a moment, which I read to you. If I could read it to you again. Just stop me if you need me to. "The exchange of prisoners shall be conducted on the one-for one basis (soldier for soldier, woman for woman, elderly person for elderly person) or on the all-for-all basis." Don't answer, but are you clear on what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have heard, and I also saw it on the monitor. Let me answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You understand my question was the meaning of the words "woman for woman and elderly person for elderly person," and I'm suggesting that it was put there to encompass situations when there was a mixture of civilians and military personnel on a list for exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief by Mr. Novak, I said that we used a copy of the East Bosnia Corps rules and that we adapted it to suit our situation, so that, as far as I can remember, we had adapted this article, and besides mentioning combatants, one for one, we had an all-for-all exchange. So when an all-for-all exchange was carried out, there is no one-for-one principle. We had our own rules, which I don't have. They stayed behind in Banja Luka. And they were rewritten and signed by our general, Momir Talic. The rules that you showed me were the rules of the East Bosnia Corps, and they were signed by General Novica Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misunderstand you. I thought your evidence was that prior to General Talic's orders coming into force, which was outside the indictment period, that is, after the 31st of December, 1993, you adapted the East Bosnia Corps regulations. Now, if you can't -- are you simply telling us -- are you simply telling us that you can't comment upon the meaning of those rules? If you can't, just tell us you can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a break in the connection, so I didn't understand everything the Prosecutor said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, which -- where is the mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Due to the technical -- the same issue that the witness just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is talking about. All right. Mr. Re, the witness didn't understand everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm simply trying to find out is the gap between when the East Bosnia Corps rules came into force in March 1993, and I think your evidence was that you adapted them until -- just let me finish -- until General Talic's came in force after the 31st of December, 1993, which is the indictment period. I'm just trying to find out which rules you used in that period, before Talic's came into force, and whether or not you can comment on that; and if you can't comment on it, that's fine. So if you'd address those two things: One, which rules did you use before 31st of December, 1993; and second, are you able to comment on it; and if not, no.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN GRUJICIC
utterances.text: I can comment to the extent that we did not get any orders from anyone to the effect that we had to draw up rules. We understood our task to be that of helping people. Our rules represented the way we behaved. When we got hold of these rules, we weren't able to rewrite them in one day. We had a lot to do. But when we had rewritten them, we gave them to the general to sign. We started our work in 1991, on the one-for-one principle or on the all-for-all principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a quarter to 2.00, Your Honours. Time for the break for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll stop our proceedings now and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
